## Main Research

By injecting information through an external synthetic data verifier, whether a human or a better model, synthetic retraining will not cause model collapse.

Recent studies raise key concerns that iteratively retraining a generative model on its self-generated synthetic data may keep deteriorating model performance, a phenomenon often coined model collapse.

## Key Approach

The paradigm advocates for verifier-based selection of synthesized data and provides criteria for when this process is successful—even with imperfect verifiers. This focuses on a scenario where synthesized data serve as the labels (answers) to questions—a common framework in tasks such as question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning.

## Theoretical Basis

Verifier-based synthetic retraining can improve performance under mild assumptions, with the underlying reason being a new form of bias–variance trade-off with bias induced by the verifier.

The research demonstrates that the key to avoiding model collapse is incorporating external verification mechanisms that introduce fresh information into the synthetic data generation process, preventing the model from deteriorating through iterative self-training cycles.

Agentic Proposing is a framework that models problem synthesis as a goal-driven sequential decision process where a specialized agent dynamically selects and composes modular reasoning skills.

The framework develops the Agentic-Proposer-4B using Multi-Granularity Policy Optimization (MGPO) to generate high-precision, verifiable training trajectories across mathematics, coding, and science. The method employs an iterative workflow of internal reflection and tool-use.

**"Preventing Curriculum Collapse in Self-Evolving Reasoning Systems"** by Vaibhav Mishra introduces **Prism**, a question-centric self-evolution method that addresses diversity collapse in self-evolving reasoning systems.

The paper focuses on self-evolving reasoning frameworks that let LLMs improve their reasoning capabilities by iteratively generating and solving problems without external supervision, using verifiable rewards. 

The key problem addressed is that self-evolving systems can exhibit diversity collapse in posing new problems after just a few iterations, even when surface-level variation is preserved.

Prism defines a persistent diversity signal over an embedding-induced semantic partition of mathematical problems and uses it to encourage balanced exploration of underrepresented regions across iterations, combined with a Zone-of-Proximal-Development (ZPD) gate to preserve edge-of-solvability difficulty.

When evaluated on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks, Prism achieved the highest accuracy on six out of seven tasks, and generated semantically diverse and challenging questions resulting in the construction of the Prism-Math dataset comprising 100k mathematical questions.

I found the paper you were looking for! Here's what the search revealed:

## Paper Overview

The paper introduces Propose, Solve, Verify (PSV), a simple self-play framework where formal verification signals are used to create a proposer capable of generating challenging synthetic problems and a solver trained via expert iteration.

## Key Problem Addressed

Training models through self-play alone without human data has been a longstanding goal in AI, but its effectiveness for training large language models remains unclear, particularly in code generation where rewards based on unit tests are brittle and prone to error propagation. The work studies self-play in the verified code generation setting, where formal verification provides reliable correctness signals.

## Main Results

The researchers used PSV to train PSV-Verus, which across three benchmarks improves pass@1 by up to 9.6x over inference-only and expert-iteration baselines.

## How It Works

At each iteration, the solver attempts to solve the current set of specifications, producing candidate solutions that are checked using formal verification. Verified solutions are used to update the solver via rejection fine-tuning, while a proposer generates new, challenging specifications using the pass rate as a proxy for what kinds of problems the solver finds difficult.

The paper was published on arXiv on December 20, 2025 (arxiv ID: 2512.18160).

The framework formulates data synthesis as a constrained information maximization problem, selecting skill combinations that maximize marginal structural information within the hierarchy while preserving semantic coherence.

The research addresses a key challenge where Large Language Models and agent-based systems struggle with compositional generalization due to a data bottleneck in which complex skill combinations follow a long-tailed, power-law distribution.
